rationale:
Evidence: iteration 1 (weights halved, kp 3, kd 0.6, base 1.4) still left the line in all 60 trials, with progress 0.04 to 0.18 and max_error about 0.061, just past the 0.06 m off-track limit. Halving the gain improved oval progress (0.115 to 0.176), so the loop is too aggressive, but the failure is still early in every track. rms_error is nearly identical across designs (about 0.03), which suggests a steady bias plus oscillation, not a single bad bend. The fixed left/right motor mismatch in the disturbance would produce a constant turn bias. With kp only, that bias leaves a steady offset of bias/(kp gain), and that offset is large enough to reach the 0.06 m limit. The control loop has no integral action to remove it.

Changes: (1) kp reduced from 3.0 to 2.0, since the earlier change showed gain is the main driver of overshoot. The sensor-to-offset slope is about 31 per metre, so the proportional turn is about 62 per metre of offset. (2) ki set to 0.3 so the integral cancels the constant mismatch bias. The integral is limited to +/-2, so windup is bounded. (3) kd raised to 0.8 to damp the oscillation that a lower kp still allows. (4) base_speed reduced to 1.3 to reduce lateral slip and the time spent in each bend. Completion in under 3 s is unlikely at this speed, but a stable run to progress near 1.0 is worth far more than the current near-zero progress (about 250 points for progress alone). (5) mass reduced to 0.6 kg to lower yaw inertia, so the robot responds faster to steering commands. Sensor layout, weights, wheel_track 0.14 and wheel_radius 0.03 are unchanged, so the effect of the gain changes can be read directly from the race.

Expected result: the robot should stay on the line through the bends, with max_error below about 0.05 m and no line-loss events. Progress should move well beyond 0.2 on all three development tracks, and completion may be reached on the oval. If the run still goes off track, the next step is to lower kp to about 1.5 or raise ki.
